stages: Who may buy, and what they can see
Before North Valley Hospital can order, it is set up as a buyer, placed in a buyer group and given entitlements. These decide which store, products and prices it sees.

The hospital account can be enabled as a buyer and assigned to a buyer group. Buyer groups connect to stores and entitlement policies, while contacts and addresses identify the people and delivery locations involved.
Sharing records control record visibility; they are not purchases. Delegated purchasing and custom sales-area relationships depend on the organization’s configuration.
The supplier's B2B store presents a catalog of categories. The Surgical Dressing Box sits under Wound Care and can carry limits on how many boxes may be bought.
A store can be associated with a catalog. Categories organize products within the catalog, and purchase quantity rules can define how products may be ordered.
History and sharing records support the catalog. Verify which store-to-catalog relationship is used and how buyer entitlements affect product visibility.
Contract prices for regional hospitals come from a price book assigned to the store and to the buyer group. Optional volume tiers can lower the unit price on larger orders.
A price book contains prices for products. Price books can be assigned to a store or buyer group, with optional schedules and tiers for price adjustments.
Price selection depends on store and buyer-group configuration. Tiered schedules are optional, and history records track changes.
Optional discounts, with or without a code

A promotion may reduce the price when the hospital qualifies, sometimes only after it enters a coupon code. Any discount then travels from the cart to the order and on to fulfillment. This path is optional.

Promotions define eligibility and targets; segments can connect them to buyer groups and stores. Coupons may trigger eligible promotions, and resulting adjustments can appear in the cart, order, or fulfillment.
Promotions are optional. How discounts carry over to orders and are allocated after a return depends on configuration.
For a large standing order, the hospital might ask for a quote before buying. A simple store purchase skips this stage entirely.
A quote may be associated with an opportunity and contains quoted product lines. It can also have a generated document and use prices from a price book.
Quotes are optional, and whether a quote becomes a store order depends on configuration. History and sharing records support the quoting process.
From a cart to a placed order
The buyer adds two Surgical Dressing Boxes, chooses a delivery option, reviews estimated tax and any warnings, and checks out.
A cart contains product lines and delivery groups. Checkout brings together delivery options, estimated tax, validation messages, inventory reservations, and payment choices as configured.
Inventory reservation and external tax, shipping, or inventory services apply only when configured.
The original order and its current view
Checkout creates the original order for two boxes. Order Management also builds a current view of the order, which later reflects shipments, cancellations and returns.
An order contains product lines and can group them for delivery. The order summary and product summaries provide a current view as the order changes.
Original orders and change orders use the same object type. The purchase-order confirmation tracker is a custom proof-of-concept object.
The boxes are picked, packed and shipped
The order is routed to a warehouse, may be picked from a pick list, and is shipped by carrier to the hospital's receiving dock.
A fulfillment order assigns work to a location and contains product lines. Pick tickets can support preparation, while shipments and shipment items describe the goods being sent.
Picking, location groups, and reservations are optional. Shipment records do not establish billing or payment; location addresses and customer addresses serve different purposes.
Tax is calculated, recorded and reduced separately
Tax is estimated in the cart, recorded on order lines, carried to fulfillment and reduced when a box is returned. Credit memo and invoice lines carry it too.
Tax policies and treatments help define how tax is calculated. Tax records can appear in the cart, order, fulfillment, and return; a provider reversal is a separate process.
Provider tax transactions and reversals are external records. A reversal must be requested and correlated through the integration; it is separate from a customer refund.
Before shipment, a quantity can be canceled. After delivery, the hospital returns one box. An exchange is another possible path but is not part of this scenario.
A return order contains lines for products being returned, with optional adjustments and tax. Processing can produce a change order and product line; a summary change records the effect on the order.
The return-to-change-order sequence is a process handoff, not an assumed direct lookup. A simple return or cancellation can create a change order without a return order.
What is owed, and what is credited
The hospital is invoiced for two boxes plus shipping and tax. After the return, a credit memo reduces what it owes by one box.
An invoice contains lines for charges. A payment can be applied to the invoice, and a credit memo can contain credit lines and be applied separately.
A posted credit is not a refund. The automation that creates invoices and credits depends on the organization’s configuration.
If the hospital pays by card, funds may be authorized and then captured. After the return, a refund can send back the money for one box. Invoiced or offline payment terms may skip authorization.
Payment methods and merchant configuration support checkout. An authorization may precede a payment; a refund can be allocated back to an earlier payment.
Gateway logs record provider interactions. A simulated gateway does not move real money, and a pending refund has not yet been processed.
When something goes wrong after delivery
The hospital may open a case about a damaged box. Support entitlements and warranties describe the help it is due. A case can lead to a return, but it does not have to.
A case can record a customer issue. Assets can carry warranty coverage, and warranty terms may be associated with products; service entitlements describe support eligibility.
A case does not necessarily link directly to a return. Service entitlements differ from commerce entitlement policies; asset tracking depends on the implementation.
Signals, logs and exceptions behind the scenes
Background jobs, events and logs record what the systems did. They help support teams investigate problems, but they are not business transactions.
Background processing and external integrations can produce operational records. Exceptions capture some failures, and change events can notify subscribers of updates.
Change events are messages rather than business records. Logs record activity and may need to be checked against the provider’s result.
